messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 42, Tane had built a steady life as an electrician, the sort of work that kept him moving between job sites and strangers’ houses, up ladders and into roof spaces, carrying tools and speaking in a calm, practical way. But after the assault, the ordinary rhythm of a day began to feel treacherous. It had happened late in the afternoon, around the same time the sun was dropping and the light in the street had gone flat. He had been outside a client’s property when a door slammed somewhere behind him and a man came at him fast, the moment breaking into fragments under the force of fear. What Tane remembered most was not a continuous story but a few sharp pictures: the shape of the man’s arm, the hard jolt of being hit, the slick, unreal sense that he was not fully there. The rest felt missing, as if the event had been cut away and only isolated frames remained. In the months afterward, whenever that same time of day came around, or whenever a door opened suddenly or slammed in the house, he felt pulled straight back toward it. At first he tried to outrun the feeling by disappearing into his phone late into the evening, losing hours to games and the internet, or by drinking to blunt the edge of the memory. He also stopped watching films or reading anything that reminded him of assaults, because even a passing scene would leave him tense for the rest of the night.

As those reminders kept landing, Tane became increasingly convinced that danger was never far away. He had come to believe that the assault said something about him, that it happened because of the sort of person he was, and that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation. The thought brought a heavy, private shame, and when he tried to remember what had happened, guilt rose immediately with it; the memory did not feel like something that had simply occurred to him, but like evidence against him. He also felt that he had no future, a bleak certainty that made the hours ahead seem empty. Those appraisals fed the way he moved through the world. He became watchful for movement near him, flinching if someone crossed behind him too quickly, and reacting with alarm when his partner touched his shoulder without warning. Unfamiliar places became hard to face, especially on workdays when he was sent to properties he had never seen before; if he could not assess the danger, he would rather avoid going at all. The more he kept scanning and bracing, the less settled he felt, and the more proof he seemed to find that the world was unsafe.

The memory itself kept reopening the injury. When a vivid flash of one of those picture-like moments came back, Tane would feel his body tighten as though the attack were starting again. That jolt of remembering made the same doors, the same hour of day, and even the faint sense of becoming detached or unreal more powerful, because they no longer felt like neutral coincidences but like signs that the event was near. In those moments he would reach for whatever could shut the experience down: more time on the phone, another drink, a pill taken longer than prescribed, any distraction that might cut through the rising alarm. Yet the long nights online and the heavier use of alcohol and medication left him foggier, more on edge, and increasingly cut off from himself. He began to think that coping this way only proved his weakness, which deepened the sense that he was the kind of man who could not manage what had happened. Even that self-judgment became another reminder, because it pulled him back to the same unfinished images and the same guilty question of what he should have done differently.

Over time the loop reached into his daily life. At work he found himself wanting to keep away from unfamiliar sites and to stay busy enough that there was no space for the memory to surface, but the constant effort to hold himself together left him jumpy and tired. A hand on the back, a sudden movement near a ladder, a door banging in a client’s garage could all make him react as if he were in danger, and once that happened he was likely to retreat into his phone or to drink that evening, both to calm himself and to stop thinking about how frightened he had looked. The avoidance, though, brought its own consequence: the more he escaped into screens, substances, and familiar media, the less confident he felt stepping back out into the world, and the more convinced he became that he was trapped in a future that had already narrowed. By the time he came to therapy, it was his partner who had pushed hardest, worried by how often he sat apart at home, staring at a screen, drinking quietly, and jumping at the simplest touch. Tane was not only afraid that the memory would return in full; he was also afraid that he had already become the kind of person who could not move beyond it. What he hoped for, even if he could barely say it aloud, was a way to walk into a doorway, hear it slam, and not feel the assault come rushing back with it.
